title: Der Frieder und das Catherlieschen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 59. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, Thür, thun, Noth, todt, ward und müßt).
about: KHM 59, a domestic farce: a chain of household catastrophes, every one of them carried out by Catherlieschen with perfect reasoning. Because her name is a diminutive, German grammar makes it neuter, and the tale slips back and forth between es, ihm, sein and the expected sie, ihr — an “it” for a grown woman that English cannot copy. Frieder’s reproach and her reply (“you should not have done that” — “you should have told me”) come back after each ruin, and the tale simply stops on a joke, with no reckoning and no moral. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as gieng, fieng, thun, Thüre, Noth and Vortheil.

sentences.t: Es war ein Mann, der hieß Frieder, und eine Frau, die hieß Catherlieschen, die hatten einander geheirathet und lebten zusammen als junge Eheleute.
sentences.l: There was a man, he was called Frieder, and a woman, she was called Catherlieschen; they had married one another and lived together as young married-folk.
sentences.i: There was once a man called Frieder and a woman called Catherlieschen; they had married one another and lived together as a young married couple.
sentences.n: geheirathet keeps the archaic th (modern geheiratet). Catherlieschen is a diminutive built on Catherlies (Katharina-Liese) — and because -chen makes a noun neuter, she is often es, ihm, sein: “it” and “its.” The tale slips back to sie and ihr as often as not. English cannot copy that, so she is “she” here.

sentences.t: Eines Tages sprach der Frieder „ich will jetzt zu Acker, Catherlieschen, wann ich wiederkomme, muß etwas Gebratenes auf dem Tisch stehen für den Hunger, und ein frischer Trunk dabei für den Durst.“
sentences.l: One day spoke the Frieder “I want now to field, Catherlieschen; when I come back, something roasted must stand on the table for the hunger, and a fresh drink beside it for the thirst.”
sentences.i: One day Frieder said: “I am off to the field now, Catherlieschen. When I come back there must be something roasted standing on the table for my hunger, and a fresh drink beside it for my thirst.”
sentences.n: “ich will jetzt zu Acker” — the verb of motion is left out after the modal: “I want [to go] to field.” Both names take the article (der Frieder, das Catherlieschen), which is village usage, not a slip. wann here stands where modern German would have wenn.

sentences.t: „Geh nur, Friederchen,“ antwortete die Catherlies, „geh nur, will dirs schon recht machen.“
sentences.l: “Just go, little-Frieder,” answered the Catherlies, “just go, will make it right for you all right.”
sentences.i: “Off you go, Friederchen,” answered Catherlies, “off you go — I shall get it right for you.”
sentences.n: The tale plays with her name: here the shorter Catherlies. schon softens a promise into reassurance — don’t worry, I will. And the subject ich is dropped from “will dirs schon recht machen”, as it is again and again whenever she speaks.

sentences.t: Als nun die Essenszeit herbeirückte, holte sie eine Wurst aus dem Schornstein, that sie in eine Bratpfanne, legte Butter dazu und stellte sie übers Feuer.
sentences.l: When now the meal-time drew near, she fetched a sausage out of the chimney, put it into a frying-pan, laid butter to it and set it over the fire.
sentences.i: Now when dinner-time drew near, she fetched a sausage out of the chimney, put it into a frying pan, added butter to it, and set it over the fire.
sentences.n: Sausages hung in the chimney to smoke and keep — the chimney was the larder. that is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun (modern tun).

sentences.t: Die Wurst fieng an zu braten und zu brutzeln, Catherlieschen stand dabei, hielt den Pfannenstiel und hatte so seine Gedanken: da fiel ihm ein „bis die Wurst fertig wird, derweil könntest du ja im Keller den Trunk zapfen.“
sentences.l: The sausage began to roast and to sizzle, Catherlieschen stood by, held the pan-handle and had so its thoughts: then it occurred to it “until the sausage is done, meanwhile you could well tap the drink in the cellar.”
sentences.i: The sausage began to fry and to sizzle; Catherlieschen stood by, holding the pan-handle, and fell to thinking — and it struck her: “While the sausage is finishing, you could be tapping the drink down in the cellar.”
sentences.n: einfallen (to occur to someone) puts the person in the dative: “da fiel ihm ein” — “it fell in to her.” She addresses herself as du, which she does every time a bright idea arrives.

sentences.t: Also stellte es den Pfannenstiel fest, nahm eine Kanne, gieng hinab in den Keller und zapfte Bier.
sentences.l: So it set the pan-handle fast, took a jug, went down into the cellar and tapped beer.
sentences.i: So she propped the pan-handle firm, took a jug, went down into the cellar and tapped beer.
sentences.n: feststellen is literal here — to fix the handle so the pan will not tip; the modern sense “to ascertain” came later.

sentences.t: Das Bier lief in die Kanne, und Catherlieschen sah ihm zu, da fiel ihm ein „holla, der Hund oben ist nicht beigethan, der könnte die Wurst aus der Pfanne holen, du kämst mir recht!“
sentences.l: The beer ran into the jug, and Catherlieschen watched it, then it occurred to it “hallo, the dog up there is not shut in, that one could fetch the sausage out of the pan, you would come to me just right!”
sentences.i: The beer ran into the jug, and Catherlieschen stood watching it — and then it struck her: “Hallo! The dog upstairs is not shut in; he could fetch the sausage out of the pan. That would suit me nicely!”
sentences.n: beithun (modern beitun) = to shut away, put by. “du kämst mir recht” is ironic — “you would come just right for me,” i.e. that is all I need; kämst is subjunctive.

sentences.t: und im Hui war es die Kellertreppe hinauf; aber der Spitz hatte die Wurst schon im Maul und schleifte sie auf der Erde mit sich fort.
sentences.l: and in a whisk it was up the cellar-stairs; but the spitz already had the sausage in its maw and was dragging it away with itself along the ground.
sentences.i: and in a flash she was up the cellar stairs — but the spitz already had the sausage in his jaws and was dragging it off along the ground.
sentences.n: “im Hui” = in a trice. The verb of motion drops out again: “war es die Kellertreppe hinauf” — “it was up the cellar stairs.” A Spitz is the sharp-nosed, curled-tail farm dog; here simply the household dog.

sentences.t: Doch Catherlieschen, nicht faul, setzte ihm nach und jagte ihn ein gut Stück ins Feld; aber der Hund war geschwinder als Catherlieschen, ließ auch die Wurst nicht fahren sondern über die Äcker hin hüpfen.
sentences.l: But Catherlieschen, not lazy, set after him and chased him a good stretch into the field; but the dog was quicker than Catherlieschen, and did not let the sausage go either, but rather let it hop away over the ploughland.
sentences.i: But Catherlieschen, quick off the mark, set off after him and chased him a good way into the field; the dog, though, was faster than Catherlieschen, and would not let the sausage go — he let it bounce along over the ploughed fields.
sentences.n: “nicht faul” (not lazy) is an idiom for “without a moment’s hesitation.” “fahren lassen” = to let go; the lassen is understood a second time with hüpfen — not let it go, but let it hop.

sentences.t: „Hin ist hin!“ sprach Catherlieschen, kehrte um, und weil es sich müde gelaufen hatte, gieng es hübsch langsam und kühlte sich ab.
sentences.l: “Gone is gone!” spoke Catherlieschen, turned about, and because it had run itself tired, it went nice and slowly and cooled itself off.
sentences.i: “Gone is gone!” said Catherlieschen, and turned back; and because she had run herself tired, she went along nice and slowly, and cooled herself down.
sentences.n: hin = away, lost: “hin ist hin” is a shrug of a proverb — what is gone is gone. “sich müde laufen” = to run oneself tired.

sentences.t: Während der Zeit lief das Bier aus dem Faß immer zu, denn Catherlieschen hatte den Hahn nicht umgedreht, und als die Kanne voll und sonst kein Platz da war, so lief es in den Keller und hörte nicht eher auf, als bis das ganze Faß leer war.
sentences.l: During that time the beer kept running out of the cask, for Catherlieschen had not turned the tap round, and when the jug was full and there was no other room, then it ran into the cellar and did not stop sooner than until the whole cask was empty.
sentences.i: All this while the beer kept running out of the cask, for Catherlieschen had not turned off the tap; and when the jug was full and there was nowhere else for it to go, it ran out over the cellar, and did not stop until the whole cask stood empty.
sentences.n: “immer zu” = on and on, without stopping. “nicht eher… als bis” = not sooner… than until, i.e. not until.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen sah schon auf der Treppe das Unglück.
sentences.l: Catherlieschen saw the disaster already on the stairs.
sentences.i: From the stairs Catherlieschen already saw the disaster.
sentences.n: schon here goes with a place rather than a time: while still on the stairs, before she reaches the cellar. Unglück covers anything from a mishap to a catastrophe.

sentences.t: „Spuk,“ rief es, „was fängst du jetzt an, daß es der Frieder nicht merkt!“
sentences.l: “Spook!” it called, “what do you begin now, so that the Frieder does not notice it!”
sentences.i: “Mercy!” she cried. “What are you to do now, so that Frieder does not notice?”
sentences.n: Spuk (a haunting, a spook) serves here as a startled oath — something like “heaven help us.” “was fängst du an” = what are you to set about, what will you do.

sentences.t: Es besann sich ein Weilchen, endlich fiel ihm ein von der letzten Kirmes stände noch ein Sack mit schönem Waitzenmehl auf dem Boden, das wollte es herabholen und in das Bier streuen.
sentences.l: It bethought itself a little-while; at last it occurred to it that from the last church-fair a sack of fine wheat-flour was still standing up in the loft — that it wanted to fetch down and strew into the beer.
sentences.i: She thought a little while, and at last it struck her that from the last church-fair a sack of fine wheat flour was still standing up in the loft; she would fetch it down and strew it into the beer.
sentences.n: stände is subjunctive — the flour is what occurred to her, reported rather than vouched for. A Kirmes is the parish fair on the church’s dedication day, when good flour was bought in. Boden here is the loft, not the ground. The source spells Waitzenmehl here and Waizenmehl a little further on; both stand as printed.

sentences.t: „Ja“, sprach es, „wer zu rechter Zeit was spart, der hats hernach in der Noth,“ stieg auf den Boden, trug den Sack herab und warf ihn gerade auf die Kanne voll Bier, daß sie umstürzte und der Trunk des Frieders auch im Keller schwamm.
sentences.l: “Yes,” it spoke, “whoever saves something at the right time, that one has it afterward in need,” climbed up to the loft, carried the sack down and threw it straight onto the jug full of beer, so that it toppled over and the Frieder’s drink swam in the cellar too.
sentences.i: “Yes,” she said, “whoever saves in good time has it by him afterwards in need,” and climbed up to the loft, carried the sack down, and threw it straight onto the jug full of beer, so that it toppled over and Frieder’s drink went swimming about the cellar as well.
sentences.n: A household proverb in the “wer… der…” shape German likes: “whoever…, he…”. Noth = modern Not, need or hardship.

sentences.t: „Es ist ganz recht,“ sprach Catherlieschen, „wo eins ist, muß das andere auch sein“ und zerstreute das Mehl im ganzen Keller.
sentences.l: “It is quite right,” spoke Catherlieschen, “where the one is, the other must be too,” and scattered the flour through the whole cellar.
sentences.i: “It is quite right,” said Catherlieschen — “where the one is, the other must be too,” and she scattered the flour all over the cellar.
sentences.n: eins … das andere = “the one … the other,” neuter indefinite pronouns for things not named. zerstreuen = to scatter about.

sentences.t: Als es fertig war, freute es sich gewaltig über seine Arbeit und sagte „wies so reinlich und sauber hier aussieht!“
sentences.l: When it was finished, it rejoiced mightily over its work and said “how tidy and clean it looks here!”
sentences.i: When she had finished she was hugely pleased with her work, and said: “How neat and clean it all looks here!”
sentences.n: wies = wie es.

sentences.t: Um Mittagszeit kam der Frieder heim.
sentences.l: About midday the Frieder came home.
sentences.i: About midday Frieder came home.

sentences.t: „Nun, Frau, was hast du mir zurecht gemacht?“
sentences.l: “Well, wife, what have you made ready for me?”
sentences.n: Frau is simply “wife” when a husband says it to her.

sentences.t: „Ach, Friederchen,“ antwortete sie, „ich wollte dir ja eine Wurst braten, aber während ich das Bier dazu zapfte, hat sie der Hund aus der Pfanne weggeholt, und während ich dem Hund nachsprang, ist das Bier ausgelaufen, und als ich das Bier mit dem Waizenmehl auftrocknen wollte, hab ich die Kanne auch noch umgestoßen; aber sei nur zufrieden, der Keller ist wieder ganz trocken.“
sentences.l: “Ah, little-Frieder,” answered she, “I did want to roast you a sausage, but while I was tapping the beer for it, the dog fetched it away out of the pan, and while I was springing after the dog, the beer ran out, and when I wanted to dry the beer up with the wheat-flour, I knocked the jug over as well; but just be content, the cellar is quite dry again.”
sentences.i: “Oh, Friederchen,” she answered, “I did mean to fry you a sausage; but while I was tapping the beer to go with it, the dog carried it off out of the pan, and while I was running after the dog the beer all ran out, and when I meant to dry the beer up with the wheat flour I knocked the jug over too. But never mind — the cellar is quite dry again.”
sentences.n: The ja in “ich wollte dir ja eine Wurst braten” is not “yes” but a small word of appeal: I really did mean to. “sei nur zufrieden” = just be content, never mind.

sentences.t: Sprach der Frieder „Catherlieschen, Catherlieschen, das hättest du nicht thun müssen! läßt die Wurst wegholen und das Bier aus dem Faß laufen, und verschüttest obendrein unser feines Mehl!“
sentences.l: Spoke the Frieder “Catherlieschen, Catherlieschen, that you should not have done! you let the sausage be fetched away and the beer run out of the cask, and spill our fine flour on top of it!”
sentences.i: Frieder said: “Catherlieschen, Catherlieschen, you should never have done that! Letting the sausage be carried off and the beer run out of the cask, and spilling our good flour into the bargain!”
sentences.n: “das hättest du nicht thun müssen” is Frieder’s refrain; it returns twice more, with sollen in place of müssen. In “läßt … verschüttest” the subject du falls away, as it does all through this tale’s dialogue, and lassen does the work English needs a passive for: lets the sausage be fetched away. obendrein = on top of it all.

sentences.t: „Ja, Friederchen, das habe ich nicht gewußt, hättest mirs sagen müssen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, little-Frieder, that I did not know, should have told it to me.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Friederchen, I did not know that — you should have told me.”
sentences.n: Her standing answer, which returns three more times, with du dropped: “hättest mirs sagen müssen.” mirs = mir es.

sentences.t: Der Mann dachte „geht das so mit deiner Frau, so mußt du dich besser vorsehen.“
sentences.l: The man thought “if it goes so with your wife, then you must look out for yourself better.”
sentences.i: The man thought: “If this is how it goes with your wife, you must be more on your guard.”
sentences.n: “geht das so” is a conditional made without wenn, by putting the verb first; the following so answers it. “sich vorsehen” = to be on one’s guard.

sentences.t: Nun hatte er eine hübsche Summe Thaler zusammen gebracht, die wechselte er in Gold ein und sprach zum Catherlieschen „siehst du, das sind gelbe Gickelinge, die will ich in einen Topf thun und im Stall unter der Kuhkrippe vergraben: aber daß du mir ja davon bleibst, sonst geht dirs schlimm.“
sentences.l: Now he had brought together a pretty sum of thalers, those he changed into gold and spoke to the Catherlieschen “do you see, those are yellow gickelings, those I will put into a pot and bury in the byre under the cow-crib: but mind that you keep away from them, otherwise it will go badly for you.”
sentences.i: Now he had put together a pretty sum in thalers; these he changed into gold, and said to Catherlieschen: “Do you see, these are yellow gickelings. I mean to put them in a pot and bury them in the byre under the cow’s manger — but mind you keep away from them, or it will go badly with you.”
sentences.n: A Thaler is the big silver coin of the day. Gickelinge is no word for money at all; Gickel is dialect for a cock, so it may be meant as something like “yellow chicks.” Either way Frieder is fobbing her off with a nonsense name, so that she will not know what she is guarding. “daß du mir ja davon bleibst” is an order dressed as a daß-clause, with mir the ethical dative (“mind me”) and ja the sharpener.

sentences.t: Sprach sie „nein, Friederchen, wills gewiß nicht thun.“
sentences.l: Spoke she “no, little-Frieder, will certainly not do it.”
sentences.i: She said: “No, Friederchen, I certainly shall not.”
sentences.n: wills = will es, with ich dropped again.

sentences.t: Nun, als der Frieder fort war, da kamen Krämer, die irdne Näpfe und Töpfe feil hatten, ins Dorf und fragten bei der jungen Frau an ob sie nichts zu handeln hätte.
sentences.l: Now, when the Frieder was away, there came pedlars into the village, who had earthen bowls and pots for sale, and enquired of the young wife whether she had nothing to trade.
sentences.i: Now when Frieder was gone, pedlars came into the village with earthenware bowls and pots for sale, and asked the young wife whether she had anything to trade.
sentences.n: “feil haben” = to have for sale (feil survives in feilbieten). irdne = irdene, earthen. “anfragen bei” = to enquire of.

sentences.t: „O, ihr lieben Leute,“ sprach Catherlieschen, „ich hab kein Geld und kann nichts kaufen; aber könnt ihr gelbe Gickelinge brauchen, so will ich wohl kaufen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, you dear people,” spoke Catherlieschen, “I have no money and can buy nothing; but if you can use yellow gickelings, then I will readily buy.”
sentences.i: “Oh, my good people,” said Catherlieschen, “I have no money and can buy nothing; but if you have any use for yellow gickelings, then I will gladly buy.”
sentences.n: “könnt ihr gelbe Gickelinge brauchen” — another conditional made without wenn, by fronting the verb.

sentences.t: „Gelbe Gickelinge, warum nicht? laßt sie einmal sehen.“
sentences.l: “Yellow gickelings, why not? let them be seen once.”
sentences.i: “Yellow gickelings — why not? Let us have a look at them.”
sentences.n: “laßt sie einmal sehen” — lassen with a bare infinitive: let them be seen, i.e. let us have a look. The einmal is the softening “just.”

sentences.t: „So geht in den Stall und grabt unter der Kuhkrippe, so werdet ihr die gelben Gickelinge finden, ich darf nicht dabei gehen.“
sentences.l: “Then go into the byre and dig under the cow-crib, then will you find the yellow gickelings; I may not go along there.”
sentences.i: “Then go into the byre and dig under the cow’s manger, and you will find the yellow gickelings. I am not allowed to go there myself.”
sentences.n: dürfen is “to be allowed,” not “to be able” — she is keeping to the letter of Frieder’s ban while breaking all of it.

sentences.t: Die Spitzbuben giengen hin, gruben und fanden eitel Gold.
sentences.l: The rogues went there, dug and found nothing but gold.
sentences.n: Spitzbube = a rascal, a thief. eitel here has its old sense “pure, nothing but,” not “vain.” The narrator quietly renames them from Krämer to Spitzbuben the moment they start digging.

sentences.t: Da packten sie auf damit, liefen fort und ließen Töpfe und Näpfe im Hause stehen.
sentences.l: Then they packed up with it, ran off and left pots and bowls standing in the house.
sentences.i: Then they packed up and made off with it, and left the pots and bowls standing in the house.
sentences.n: aufpacken is to load up, to shoulder a load: “packten … auf damit” = they loaded up with it. Näpfe are bowls or basins, Töpfe the pots.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen meinte sie müßte das neue Geschirr auch brauchen: weil nun in der Küche ohnehin kein Mangel daran war, schlug sie jedem Topf den Boden aus und steckte sie insgesammt zum Zierrath auf die Zaunpfähle rings ums Haus herum.
sentences.l: Catherlieschen thought she must make use of the new crockery too: because now in the kitchen there was no lack of it anyway, she knocked the bottom out of every pot and stuck them all together onto the fence-posts round about the house, for ornament.
sentences.i: Catherlieschen thought she ought to make some use of the new crockery too; and since there was no shortage of it in the kitchen anyway, she knocked the bottom out of every pot and stuck them all on the fence-posts round the house, for ornament.
sentences.n: müßte is subjunctive inside what she supposed. “den Boden ausschlagen” = to knock the bottom out. insgesammt = modern insgesamt, all together; Zierrath = modern Zierat, ornament.

sentences.t: Wie der Frieder kam, und den neuen Zierrath sah, sprach er „Catherlieschen, was hast du gemacht?“
sentences.l: When the Frieder came, and saw the new ornament, he spoke “Catherlieschen, what have you done?”
sentences.i: When Frieder came and saw the new ornament, he said: “Catherlieschen, what have you done?”
sentences.n: wie at the head of a clause is “when,” not “how” or “as” — a common older use that runs through this tale. Zierrath (modern Zierat) = decoration, ornament.

sentences.t: „Habs gekauft, Friederchen, für die gelben Gickelinge, die unter der Kuhkrippe steckten: bin selber nicht dabei gegangen, die Krämer haben sichs heraus graben müssen.“
sentences.l: “Bought it, little-Frieder, for the yellow gickelings that were stuck under the cow-crib: went not along there myself, the pedlars had to dig it out for themselves.”
sentences.i: “I bought it, Friederchen, with the yellow gickelings that were lying under the cow’s manger. I did not go there myself — the pedlars had to dig it out for themselves.”
sentences.n: Habs = habe es; and again the subject falls away at the head of both clauses — the clipped, hurried voice the tale gives her.

sentences.t: „Ach, Frau,“ sprach der Frieder, „was hast du gemacht! das waren keine Gickelinge, es war eitel Gold und war all unser Vermögen; das hättest du nicht thun sollen.“
sentences.l: “Ah, wife,” spoke the Frieder, “what have you done! those were no gickelings, it was pure gold and was all our fortune; that you should not have done.”
sentences.i: “Oh, wife,” said Frieder, “what have you done! Those were no gickelings; it was pure gold, and it was all we had. You should never have done that.”

sentences.t: „Ja, Friederchen,“ antwortete sie, „das hab ich nicht gewußt, hättest mirs vorher sagen sollen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, little-Frieder,” answered she, “that I did not know, should have told it to me beforehand.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Friederchen,” she answered, “I did not know that — you should have told me beforehand.”

sentences.t: Catherlieschen stand ein Weilchen und besann sich, da sprach sie „hör, Friederchen, das Gold wollen wir schon wieder kriegen, wollen hinter den Dieben herlaufen.“
sentences.l: Catherlieschen stood a little-while and bethought itself, then she spoke “listen, little-Frieder, the gold we shall get back all right; let us run after the thieves.”
sentences.i: Catherlieschen stood a little while and thought, and then said: “Listen, Friederchen, we shall get the gold back right enough; let us run after the thieves.”
sentences.n: “hinter jemandem herlaufen” = to run along after someone. schon again as reassurance: never fear, we shall.

sentences.t: „So komm,“ sprach der Frieder, „wir wollens versuchen; nimm aber Butter und Käse mit, daß wir auf dem Weg was zu essen haben.“
sentences.l: “Then come,” spoke the Frieder, “we will try it; but take butter and cheese along, so that we have something to eat on the way.”
sentences.n: wollens = wollen es. The daß-clause is a purpose clause — so that we have something to eat; modern German would as readily use damit.

sentences.t: „Ja, Friederchen, wills mitnehmen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, little-Frieder, will take it along.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Friederchen, I shall bring them.”

sentences.t: Sie machten sich fort, und weil der Frieder besser zu Fuß war, gieng Catherlieschen hinten nach.
sentences.l: They made themselves off, and because the Frieder was better on foot, Catherlieschen went along behind.
sentences.i: They set off; and because Frieder was the better walker, Catherlieschen came along behind.
sentences.n: “gut zu Fuß sein” = to be a good walker.

sentences.t: „Ist mein Vortheil“ dachte es, „wenn wir umkehren, hab ich ja ein Stück voraus.“
sentences.l: “Is my advantage,” thought it, “when we turn back, I have a stretch ahead after all.”
sentences.i: “That is to my advantage,” she thought; “when we turn back, I shall be a good stretch ahead.”
sentences.n: Vortheil = modern Vorteil, with the archaic th. Her reasoning is impeccable and useless — which is the tale’s whole method.

sentences.t: Nun kam es an einen Berg, wo auf beiden Seiten des Wegs tiefe Fahrgleisen waren.
sentences.l: Now it came to a hill, where on both sides of the way there were deep wheel-ruts.
sentences.i: Now she came to a hill, where on both sides of the road there were deep wheel-ruts.
sentences.n: Fahrgleise are the ruts worn by cart wheels, from fahren and Gleis (track); Fahrgleisen is the older plural.

sentences.t: „Da sehe einer,“ sprach Catherlieschen, „was sie das arme Erdreich zerrissen, geschunden und gedrückt haben! das wird sein Lebtag nicht wieder heil.“
sentences.l: “Let one look at that,” spoke Catherlieschen, “how they have torn, flayed and pressed the poor earth! that will not be whole again its life-long.”
sentences.i: “Only look at that,” said Catherlieschen, “how they have torn and flayed and crushed the poor ground! It will never be whole again as long as it lives.”
sentences.n: “da sehe einer” — an impersonal subjunctive of exclamation: let a person just look at that. “sein Lebtag” = all its born days. Erdreich is the soil as a body, which is what lets her pity it.

sentences.t: Und aus mitleidigem Herzen nahm es seine Butter und bestrich die Gleisen, rechts und links, damit sie von den Rädern nicht so gedrückt würden: und wie es sich bei seiner Barmherzigkeit so bückte, rollte ihm ein Käse aus der Tasche den Berg hinab.
sentences.l: And out of a pitying heart it took its butter and smeared the ruts, right and left, so that they should not be pressed so hard by the wheels: and as it bent down so at its work of mercy, a cheese rolled out of its pocket down the hill.
sentences.i: And out of a pitying heart she took her butter and smeared the ruts, right and left, so that the wheels should not press them so hard; and as she stooped over her work of mercy, a cheese rolled out of her pocket and away down the hill.
sentences.n: würden makes the purpose-clause hypothetical: so that they should not be pressed. Barmherzigkeit is a churchly word — mercy, compassion — used here with a perfectly straight face.

sentences.t: Sprach das Catherlieschen „ich habe den Weg schon einmal herauf gemacht, ich gehe nicht wieder hinab, es mag ein anderer hinlaufen und ihn wieder holen.“
sentences.l: Spoke the Catherlieschen “I have made the way up here once already, I am not going down again, another may run there and fetch it back.”
sentences.i: Catherlieschen said: “I have come up this road once already; I am not going down again. Let another run down and fetch it back.”
sentences.n: mögen here is “may, let” — a permission granted, not a wish.

sentences.t: Also nahm es einen andern Käs und rollte ihn hinab.
sentences.l: So it took another cheese and rolled it down.
sentences.i: So she took a second cheese and rolled it down as well.
sentences.n: Käs is the clipped form of Käse.

sentences.t: Die Käse aber kamen nicht wieder, da ließ es noch einen dritten hinablaufen und dachte „vielleicht warten sie auf Gesellschaft und gehen nicht gern allein.“
sentences.l: But the cheeses did not come back, so it let a third one run down as well and thought “perhaps they are waiting for company and do not like to go alone.”
sentences.n: “warten auf” takes the accusative: to wait for. Gesellschaft here is company, someone to go along with.

sentences.t: Als sie alle drei ausblieben, sprach es „ich weiß nicht was das vorstellen soll! doch kanns ja sein, der dritte hat den Weg nicht gefunden, und sich verirrt, ich will nur den vierten schicken, daß er sie herbei ruft.“
sentences.l: When all three of them stayed away, it spoke “I do not know what that is supposed to mean! yet it may well be the third has not found the way, and has gone astray; I will just send the fourth, so that he calls them over.”
sentences.i: When all three stayed away, she said: “I do not know what this is meant to be! Still, it may be that the third did not find the road and lost his way. I shall just send the fourth, to call them back.”
sentences.n: “was das vorstellen soll” = what that is supposed to represent, what it is meant to be. kanns = kann es.

sentences.t: Der vierte machte es aber nicht besser als der dritte.
sentences.l: But the fourth did it no better than the third.

sentences.t: Da ward das Catherlieschen ärgerlich und warf noch den fünften und sechsten hinab, und das waren die letzten.
sentences.l: Then the Catherlieschen grew annoyed and threw the fifth and sixth down as well, and those were the last.
sentences.n: ward is the old preterite of werden (modern wurde): grew, became. ärgerlich = annoyed, put out.

sentences.t: Eine Zeit lang blieb es stehen und lauerte daß sie kämen, als sie aber immer nicht kamen, sprach es „o, ihr seid gut nach dem Tod schicken, ihr bleibt fein lange aus; meint ihr ich wollt noch länger auf euch warten? ich gehe meiner Wege, ihr könnt mir nachlaufen, ihr habt jüngere Beine als ich.“
sentences.l: For a while it stood still and watched for them to come; but as they still did not come, it spoke “oh, you are good to send after death, you stay away a fine long time; do you think I would wait for you any longer? I go my ways, you can run after me, you have younger legs than I.”
sentences.i: For a while she stood still and watched for them to come; but when they still did not come, she said: “Oh, you are the ones to send for death — you stay away a fine long time. Do you suppose I mean to wait for you any longer? I am going my way; you can run after me, you have younger legs than I have.”
sentences.n: “gut nach dem Tod schicken sein” is a proverbial jibe: you are the right one to send to fetch Death, because you would take so long about it that he would never arrive. “meiner Wege gehen” is a genitive idiom — to go one’s way.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen gieng fort und fand den Frieder, der war stehen geblieben, und hatte gewartet, weil er gerne was essen wollte.
sentences.l: Catherlieschen went off and found the Frieder; he had stopped, and had waited, because he wanted gladly to eat something.
sentences.i: Catherlieschen went on and found Frieder; he had stopped and waited, because he was ready for something to eat.
sentences.n: The der in “der war stehen geblieben” is a demonstrative picking Frieder up again, where English would use “who.” “stehen bleiben” = to stop, stay standing.

sentences.t: „Nun, gib einmal her, was du mitgenommen hast.“
sentences.l: “Well, hand over now what you have brought along.”
sentences.n: “gib her” = hand it over; einmal (often shortened to mal) softens an order into a “just.”

sentences.t: Sie reichte ihm das trockne Brot.
sentences.l: She handed him the dry bread.

sentences.t: „Wo ist Butter und Käse?“ fragte der Mann.
sentences.l: “Where are butter and cheese?” asked the man.
sentences.n: “wo ist Butter und Käse” — with the verb in front the agreement follows the nearer subject and stays singular; modern usage would prefer sind.

sentences.t: „Ach, Friederchen,“ sagte Catherlieschen, „mit der Butter hab ich die Fahrgleisen geschmiert, und die Käse werden bald kommen; einer lief mir fort, da hab ich die andern nachgeschickt, sie sollten ihn rufen.“
sentences.l: “Ah, little-Frieder,” said Catherlieschen, “with the butter I have greased the wheel-ruts, and the cheeses will come soon; one ran away on me, so I sent the others after it, they were to call it.”
sentences.i: “Oh, Friederchen,” said Catherlieschen, “I greased the wheel-ruts with the butter, and the cheeses will be along presently. One ran off on me, so I sent the others after him to call him back.”
sentences.n: “einer lief mir fort” — mir is the dative of loss again: it ran off on me.

sentences.t: Sprach der Frieder „das hättest du nicht thun sollen, Catherlieschen, die Butter an den Weg schmieren und die Käse den Berg hinab rollen.“
sentences.l: Spoke the Frieder “that you should not have done, Catherlieschen — smear the butter on the road and roll the cheeses down the hill.”
sentences.i: Frieder said: “You should never have done that, Catherlieschen — greasing the road with the butter and rolling the cheeses down the hill.”
sentences.n: The two infinitives at the end, “die Butter … schmieren” and “die Käse … rollen,” stand in apposition to the das at the front: that — namely, smearing and rolling.

sentences.t: „Ja, Friederchen, hättest mirs sagen müssen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, little-Frieder, should have told it to me.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Friederchen, you should have told me.”

sentences.t: Da aßen sie das trockne Brot zusammen, und der Frieder sagte „Catherlieschen, hast du auch unser Haus verwahrt, wie du fort gegangen bist?“
sentences.l: Then they ate the dry bread together, and the Frieder said “Catherlieschen, did you make our house secure too, when you went away?”
sentences.i: Then they ate the dry bread together, and Frieder said: “Catherlieschen, did you make our house fast when you left?”
sentences.n: auch in a question is a check on the answer: you did, I hope? verwahren = to make fast, secure.

sentences.t: „Nein, Friederchen, hättest mirs vorher sagen sollen.“
sentences.l: “No, little-Frieder, should have told it to me beforehand.”
sentences.i: “No, Friederchen, you should have told me beforehand.”

sentences.t: „So geh wieder heim und bewahr erst das Haus, ehe wir weiter gehen; bring auch etwas anderes zu essen mit, ich will hier auf dich warten.“
sentences.l: “Then go home again and guard the house first, before we go further; bring something else to eat along too, I will wait here for you.”
sentences.i: “Then go back home and make the house fast first, before we go on; and bring something else to eat, and I will wait for you here.”
sentences.n: ehe is the older “before” (modern bevor). Frieder says bewahren here for the verwahren of a moment ago — a hair’s breadth apart, and Catherlieschen takes whichever word she is given as literally as it will bear.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen gieng zurück und dachte „Friederchen will etwas anderes zu essen, Butter und Käse schmeckt ihm wohl nicht, so will ich ein Tuch voll Hutzeln und einen Krug Essig zum Trunk mitnehmen.“
sentences.l: Catherlieschen went back and thought “little-Frieder wants something else to eat, butter and cheese do not taste good to him, so I will take along a cloth full of dried-pears and a jug of vinegar for the drink.”
sentences.i: Catherlieschen went back, thinking: “Friederchen wants something else to eat; butter and cheese are not to his taste. So I shall take a cloth full of dried pears, and a jug of vinegar for the drink.”
sentences.n: Hutzeln are dried pears — a country keeping-food. “schmeckt ihm” puts the taster in the dative: it tastes good to him.

sentences.t: Danach riegelte es die Oberthüre zu, aber die Unterthüre hob es aus, nahm sie auf die Schulter und glaubte wenn es die Thüre in Sicherheit gebracht hätte, müßte das Haus wohl bewahrt sein.
sentences.l: After that it bolted the upper-door shut, but the lower-door it lifted out, took it on its shoulder and believed that if it had brought the door into safety, the house must surely be secured.
sentences.i: After that she bolted the upper door, but lifted the lower door off its hinges, took it on her shoulder, and believed that if she had the door in safety the house must surely be safe.
sentences.n: The doorway has two leaves, an Oberthüre and an Unterthüre, so that the top may stand open while the bottom keeps the animals out. Thüre = modern Tür, with the archaic th. “ausheben” = to lift a door off its hinges.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen nahm sich Zeit zum Weg und dachte, „desto länger ruht sich Friederchen aus.“
sentences.l: Catherlieschen took itself time for the way and thought, “so much the longer little-Frieder rests himself.”
sentences.i: Catherlieschen took her time on the road, thinking: “All the longer for Friederchen to rest.”
sentences.n: desto = so much the (more, longer); it usually answers a je, but here it stands alone.

sentences.t: Als es ihn wieder erreicht hatte, sprach es „da, Friederchen, hast du die Hausthüre, da kannst du das Haus selber verwahren.“
sentences.l: When it had reached him again, it spoke “there, little-Frieder, you have the house-door, there you can secure the house yourself.”
sentences.i: When she had caught him up again, she said: “There, Friederchen, there is the house door; now you can make the house fast yourself.”
sentences.n: da twice as a handing-over word rather than a place: there, you have it; there, now you can. verwahren = to make fast, to secure — Frieder’s own word.

sentences.t: „Ach, Gott,“ sprach er, „was hab ich für eine kluge Frau! hebt die Thüre unten aus, daß alles hinein laufen kann, und riegelt sie oben zu.
sentences.l: “Ah, God,” spoke he, “what a clever wife have I! lifts the door out below, so that everything can run in, and bolts it shut above.
sentences.i: “Ah, Lord,” he said, “what a clever wife I have! Lifts the door out below, so that anything at all can walk in, and bolts it shut above.
sentences.n: “was hab ich für eine kluge Frau” means the opposite of what it says. The verbs then run on with no subject at all: (she) lifts, (she) bolts.

sentences.t: Jetzt ists zu spät noch einmal nach Haus zu gehen, aber hast du die Thüre hierher gebracht, so sollst du sie auch ferner tragen.“
sentences.l: Now it is too late to go home once more; but have you brought the door here, then shall you carry it further too.”
sentences.i: Now it is too late to go home again; but since you have brought the door this far, you shall carry it further too.”
sentences.n: “hast du die Thüre hierher gebracht” — a third conditional made by fronting the verb: “if you have brought…”. ferner = further, on from here.

sentences.t: „Die Thüre will ich tragen, Friederchen, aber die Hutzeln und der Essigkrug werden mir zu schwer: ich hänge sie an die Thüre, die mag sie tragen.“
sentences.l: “The door I will carry, little-Frieder, but the dried-pears and the vinegar-jug are becoming too heavy for me: I hang them on the door, that one may carry them.”
sentences.i: “The door I will carry, Friederchen, but the dried pears and the vinegar jug are growing too heavy for me. I shall hang them on the door — the door may carry them.”
sentences.n: “werden mir zu schwer” puts the person in the dative: they are growing too heavy for me. mag here is “may, let” — let the door carry them.

sentences.t: Nun giengen sie in den Wald und suchten die Spitzbuben, aber sie fanden sie nicht.
sentences.l: Now they went into the forest and looked for the rogues, but they did not find them.
sentences.n: Two sie in a row with different owners: the first is the pair, the second the rogues. German leaves them to be sorted by sense.

sentences.t: Weils endlich dunkel ward, stiegen sie auf einen Baum und wollten da übernachten.
sentences.l: Because it grew dark at last, they climbed up a tree and meant to spend the night there.
sentences.n: Weils = weil es.

sentences.t: Kaum aber saßen sie oben, so kamen die Kerle daher, die forttragen was nicht mitgehen will, und die Dinge finden, ehe sie verloren sind.
sentences.l: But scarcely were they sitting up there, when there came along the fellows who carry off what will not come along by itself, and who find things before they are lost.
sentences.i: But scarcely were they up there when along came the fellows who carry off whatever will not walk off by itself, and who find things before they are lost.
sentences.n: A proverbial joke-definition of thieves, delivered deadpan as though it were an ordinary description. “kaum… so…” = scarcely… when…

sentences.t: Sie ließen sich gerade unter dem Baum nieder, auf dem Frieder und Catherlieschen saßen, machten sie ein Feuer an und wollten ihre Beute theilen.
sentences.l: They settled themselves down right under the tree on which Frieder and Catherlieschen sat, made a fire and meant to divide their booty.
sentences.i: They settled down right under the tree on which Frieder and Catherlieschen were sitting, lit a fire, and set about dividing their booty.
sentences.n: “sich niederlassen” = to settle down. In “machten sie ein Feuer an” the subject is repeated where the coordinate clause does not need it. theilen = modern teilen.

sentences.t: Der Frieder stieg von der andern Seite herab und sammelte Steine, stieg damit wieder hinauf und wollte die Diebe todt werfen.
sentences.l: The Frieder climbed down on the other side and gathered stones, climbed up again with them and meant to throw the thieves dead.
sentences.i: Frieder climbed down the other side and gathered stones, climbed up again with them, and meant to stone the thieves to death.
sentences.n: “todt werfen” — to throw at someone until he is dead, on the same pattern as todtschlagen, to strike dead.

sentences.t: Die Steine aber trafen nicht, und die Spitzbuben riefen „es ist bald Morgen, der Wind schüttelt die Tannäpfel herunter.“
sentences.l: But the stones did not hit, and the rogues called “it is nearly morning, the wind is shaking the fir-cones down.”
sentences.n: Tannäpfel (“fir-apples”) = fir cones, modern Tannenzapfen.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen hatte die Thüre noch immer auf der Schulter, und weil sie so schwer drückte, dachte es die Hutzeln wären schuld und sprach „Friederchen, ich muß die Hutzeln hinabwerfen.“
sentences.l: Catherlieschen still had the door on its shoulder, and because it pressed so heavily, it thought the dried-pears were to blame and spoke “little-Frieder, I must throw the dried-pears down.”
sentences.i: Catherlieschen still had the door on her shoulder; and because it bore down so heavily, she thought the dried pears were to blame, and said: “Friederchen, I must throw the dried pears down.”
sentences.n: wären is subjunctive — what she supposed, not what was so. The door, of course, is what is heavy.

sentences.t: „Nein, Catherlieschen, jetzt nicht,“ antwortete er, „sie könnten uns verrathen.“
sentences.l: “No, Catherlieschen, not now,” answered he, “they could betray us.”
sentences.n: verrathen = modern verraten.

sentences.t: „Ach, Friederchen, ich muß, sie drücken mich gar zu sehr.“
sentences.l: “Ah, little-Frieder, I must, they press me far too much.”
sentences.i: “Oh, Friederchen, I must — they weigh on me far too much.”
sentences.n: “gar zu sehr” = far too much; gar before zu strengthens, rather than the “even, quite” it is elsewhere. drücken here is physical, to bear down on.

sentences.t: „Nun so thus, ins Henkers Namen!“
sentences.l: “Well then do it, in the hangman’s name!”
sentences.n: thus = thu es (modern tu es). “ins Henkers Namen” is a mock-oath on the pattern of “in Gottes Namen” — go on then, and the hangman take it; ins is a contraction of in des.

sentences.t: Da rollten die Hutzeln zwischen den Ästen herab, und die Kerle unten sprachen „die Vögel misten.“
sentences.l: Then the dried-pears rolled down between the branches, and the fellows below spoke “the birds are dunging.”
sentences.i: Then the dried pears came rolling down through the branches, and the fellows below said: “The birds are dropping their dirt.”
sentences.n: misten, of birds, is to drop dung. Each interruption from above gets explained away as weather or nature: cones, droppings, dew.

sentences.t: Eine Weile danach, weil die Thüre noch immer drückte, sprach Catherlieschen „ach, Friederchen, ich muß den Essig ausschütten.“
sentences.l: A while after that, because the door was still pressing, Catherlieschen spoke “ah, little-Frieder, I must pour the vinegar out.”
sentences.i: A while later, because the door was still bearing down on her, Catherlieschen said: “Oh, Friederchen, I must pour the vinegar out.”

sentences.t: „Nein, Catherlieschen, das darfst du nicht, es könnte uns verrathen.“
sentences.l: “No, Catherlieschen, that you may not do, it could betray us.”

sentences.t: „Ach, Friederchen, ich muß, er drückt mich gar zu sehr.“
sentences.l: “Ah, little-Frieder, I must, it presses me far too much.”
sentences.i: “Oh, Friederchen, I must — it weighs on me far too much.”
sentences.n: er here is the vinegar: German pronouns follow the gender of the noun (der Essig), not the English sense of “it.”

sentences.t: „Nun so thus ins Henkers Namen!“
sentences.l: “Well then do it in the hangman’s name!”

sentences.t: Da schüttete es den Essig aus, daß er die Kerle bespritzte.
sentences.l: Then it poured the vinegar out, so that it spattered the fellows.
sentences.i: Then she poured the vinegar out, so that it spattered the fellows below.

sentences.t: Sie sprachen unter einander „der Thau tröpfelt schon herunter.“
sentences.l: They spoke among one another “the dew is already dripping down.”
sentences.i: They said to one another: “The dew is beginning to drip already.”
sentences.n: Thau = modern Tau, dew.

sentences.t: Endlich dachte Catherlieschen „sollte es wohl die Thüre sein, was mich so drückt?“ und sprach „Friederchen, ich muß die Thüre hinabwerfen.“
sentences.l: At last Catherlieschen thought “could it perhaps be the door that presses me so?” and spoke “little-Frieder, I must throw the door down.”
sentences.i: At last Catherlieschen thought: “Could it be the door that is weighing on me so?” — and said: “Friederchen, I must throw the door down.”
sentences.n: “sollte es wohl… sein” — sollen in the subjunctive for a guess: could it possibly be. It has taken her the whole night to arrive at it.

sentences.t: „Nein, Catherlieschen, jetzt nicht, sie könnte uns verrathen.“
sentences.l: “No, Catherlieschen, not now, it could betray us.”
sentences.n: The pronoun follows German gender: sie könnte here is die Thüre; earlier sie könnten was die Hutzeln (plural), and es könnte pointed at the act, not at der Essig.

sentences.t: „Ach, Friederchen, ich muß, sie drückt mich gar zu sehr.“
sentences.l: “Ah, little-Frieder, I must, it presses me far too much.”
sentences.i: “Oh, Friederchen, I must — it weighs on me far too much.”

sentences.t: „Nein, Catherlieschen, halt sie ja fest.“
sentences.l: “No, Catherlieschen, do hold it fast.”
sentences.n: ja sharpens the command: mind you hold it.

sentences.t: „Ach, Friederchen, ich laß sie fallen.“
sentences.l: “Ah, little-Frieder, I am letting it fall.”
sentences.n: “fallen lassen” = to let fall, to drop; laß drops its final -e as speech does. The present tense reports what is already happening, not a threat.

sentences.t: „Ei,“ antwortete Frieder ärgerlich, „so laß sie fallen ins Teufels Namen!“
sentences.l: “Eh,” answered Frieder crossly, “then let it fall in the devil’s name!”
sentences.n: The mock-oath has climbed from the hangman to the devil — which is precisely what the men below take it for.

sentences.t: Da fiel sie herunter mit starkem Gepolter, und die Kerle unten riefen „der Teufel kommt vom Baum herab,“ rissen aus und ließen alles im Stich.
sentences.l: Then it fell down with a great clattering, and the fellows below called “the devil is coming down from the tree,” tore off and left everything in the lurch.
sentences.i: Then down it came with a great crash, and the fellows below cried, “The devil is coming down out of the tree!” — and they bolted, and left the whole lot behind.
sentences.n: “ausreißen” = to bolt, to run for it. “im Stich lassen” = to leave in the lurch, to abandon.

sentences.t: Frühmorgens, wie die zwei herunter kamen, fanden sie all ihr Gold wieder und trugens heim.
sentences.l: Early in the morning, when the two came down, they found all their gold again and carried it home.
sentences.n: trugens = trugen es.

sentences.t: Als sie wieder zu Haus waren, sprach der Frieder „Catherlieschen, nun mußt du aber auch fleißig sein und arbeiten.“
sentences.l: When they were at home again, the Frieder spoke “Catherlieschen, now you really must be diligent and work.”
sentences.i: When they were home again, Frieder said: “Catherlieschen, now you must be industrious and work as well.”
sentences.n: aber auch together make a mild insistence — now you really must. fleißig sein is to keep steadily at work.

sentences.t: „Ja, Friederchen, wills schon thun, will ins Feld gehen, Frucht schneiden.“
sentences.l: “Yes, little-Frieder, will do it right enough, will go into the field, cut grain.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Friederchen, I shall do it; I shall go into the field and cut the grain.”
sentences.n: Frucht here is the standing corn, the grain crop, not fruit.

sentences.t: Als Catherlieschen im Feld war, sprachs mit sich selber „eß ich, eh ich schneid, oder schlaf ich, eh ich schneid? hei, ich will ehr essen!“
sentences.l: When Catherlieschen was in the field, it spoke with itself “do I eat before I cut, or do I sleep before I cut? ho, I will eat first!”
sentences.i: When Catherlieschen was in the field, she said to herself: “Do I eat before I cut, or do I sleep before I cut? Ho — I will eat first!”
sentences.n: sprachs = sprach es. eh = ehe, before; schneid drops its final -e, as speech does. ehr is a dialect form of eher, sooner, first.

sentences.t: Da aß Catherlieschen und ward überm Essen schläfrig, und fieng an zu schneiden und schnitt halb träumend alle seine Kleider entzwei, Schürze, Rock und Hemd.
sentences.l: So Catherlieschen ate and became sleepy over the eating, and began to cut and cut all its clothes in two, half dreaming — apron, skirt and shift.
sentences.i: So Catherlieschen ate, and grew sleepy over her eating, and began to cut, and half in a dream cut all her clothes in two — apron, skirt and shift.
sentences.n: “überm Essen” = over the eating, in the course of the meal. Hemd is the long linen undershirt worn next to the skin.

sentences.t: Wie Catherlieschen nach langem Schlaf wieder erwachte, stand es halb nackigt da und sprach zu sich selber „bin ichs, oder bin ichs nicht? ach, ich bins nicht!“
sentences.l: When Catherlieschen woke again after a long sleep, it stood there half naked and spoke to itself “am I it, or am I not it? ah, I am not it!”
sentences.i: When Catherlieschen woke again after a long sleep, she stood there half naked and said to herself: “Am I me, or am I not? Oh — I am not me!”
sentences.n: nackigt is a homely form of nackt. bin ichs = bin ich es; bins = bin es — “am I it,” with es standing in for her own identity. The riddle is a wandering folk joke, and she settles it in the next breath by asking her husband.

sentences.t: Unterdessen wards Nacht, da lief Catherlieschen ins Dorf hinein, klopfte an ihres Mannes Fenster und rief „Friederchen?“
sentences.l: Meanwhile it became night, so Catherlieschen ran into the village, knocked at her husband’s window and called “Friederchen?”
sentences.i: Meanwhile night came on, and Catherlieschen ran into the village, knocked at her husband’s window and called: “Friederchen?”
sentences.n: wards = ward es. “ihres Mannes Fenster” sets the genitive before its noun, a stately older word order.

sentences.t: „Was ist denn?“
sentences.l: “What is it, then?”

sentences.t: „Möcht gern wissen, ob Catherlieschen drinnen ist.“
sentences.l: “Should like to know whether Catherlieschen is inside.”
sentences.i: “I should like to know whether Catherlieschen is inside.”
sentences.n: “möcht gern wissen” = I should like to know — möchte with gern is the ordinary way to put it. The ich is dropped, as whenever she talks to herself.

sentences.t: „Ja, ja,“ antwortete der Frieder, „es wird wohl drinn liegen und schlafen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, yes,” answered the Frieder, “it will surely be lying inside and sleeping.”
sentences.i: “Yes, yes,” answered Frieder, “she will be lying inside asleep.”
sentences.n: “es wird wohl liegen” — werden with an infinitive here is a guess about the present, not a future: she is probably lying there. drinn = modern drin.

sentences.t: Sprach sie „gut, dann bin ich gewiß schon zu Haus“ und lief fort.
sentences.l: Spoke she “good, then I am certainly at home already,” and ran off.
sentences.i: “Good,” said she, “then I am surely at home already” — and ran off.

sentences.t: Draußen fand Catherlieschen Spitzbuben, die wollten stehlen.
sentences.l: Outside Catherlieschen found rogues who meant to steal.
sentences.n: die wollten stehlen — die is a demonstrative doing relative duty (“who”), and wollen here is “meant to, were about to,” not “wanted.”

sentences.t: Da gieng es bei sie und sprach „ich will euch helfen stehlen.“
sentences.l: So it went up to them and spoke “I will help you steal.”
sentences.i: So she went up to them and said: “I will help you steal.”
sentences.n: “bei sie”, with the accusative after bei, is regional; standard German would say “zu ihnen”.

sentences.t: Die Spitzbuben meinten es wüßte die Gelegenheit des Orts und warens zufrieden.
sentences.l: The rogues thought it knew the lie of the place and were content with it.
sentences.i: The rogues supposed she knew the lie of the place, and were content.
sentences.n: wüßte is subjunctive — what they supposed, not what was so. “die Gelegenheit des Orts” = how the place lies, what stands where. warens = waren es.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen gieng vor die Häuser und rief „Leute, habt ihr was? wir wollen stehlen.“
sentences.l: Catherlieschen went in front of the houses and called “people, have you anything? we mean to steal.”

sentences.t: Dachten die Spitzbuben „das wird gut werden“ und wünschten sie wären Catherlieschen wieder los.
sentences.l: Thought the rogues “this will turn out well,” and wished they were rid of Catherlieschen again.
sentences.i: The rogues thought, “This will turn out nicely,” and wished they were rid of Catherlieschen again.
sentences.n: “los sein” = to be rid of; wären is the subjunctive of the wish.

sentences.t: Da sprachen sie zu ihm „vorm Dorfe hat der Pfarrer Rüben auf dem Feld, geh hin und rupf uns Rüben.“
sentences.l: Then they spoke to it “outside the village the parson has turnips in the field, go there and pull us turnips.”
sentences.i: So they said to her: “Out beyond the village the parson has turnips in his field; go and pull us some turnips.”
sentences.n: The Pfarrer is the parish priest, whose glebe land lay just outside the village.

sentences.t: Catherlieschen gieng hin aufs Land und fieng an zu rupfen, war aber so faul, und hob sich nicht in die Höhe.
sentences.l: Catherlieschen went off there onto the land and began to pull, but was so lazy, and did not raise itself up into the height.
sentences.i: Catherlieschen went off to the field and began to pull, but was so lazy that she never straightened up at all.
sentences.n: Land here is the piece of ground, the field. “sich in die Höhe heben” = to raise oneself upright.

sentences.t: Da kam ein Mann vorbei, sahs und stand still und dachte, das wäre der Teufel, der so in den Rüben wühlte.
sentences.l: Then a man came past, saw it and stood still and thought that was the devil rooting about so in the turnips.
sentences.i: Then a man came by, saw it, and stood still, and thought it was the devil rooting about there in the turnips.
sentences.n: sahs = sah es. wäre is subjunctive: what he took it for.

sentences.t: Lief fort ins Dorf zum Pfarrer und sprach „Herr Pfarrer, in eurem Rübenland ist der Teufel und rupft.“
sentences.l: Ran off into the village to the parson and spoke “master parson, in your turnip-land is the devil, and is pulling.”
sentences.i: He ran off into the village to the parson and said: “Master parson, the devil is in your turnip field, pulling them up.”
sentences.n: The subject drops away at the head of the sentence — “(he) ran off” — as it does whenever this tale is in a hurry. eurem is the old respectful “your” addressed to a man of standing.

sentences.t: „Ach Gott,“ antwortete der Pfarrer, „ich habe einen lahmen Fuß, ich kann nicht hinaus und ihn wegbannen.“
sentences.l: “Ah God,” answered the parson, “I have a lame foot, I cannot out and banish him away.”
sentences.i: “Ah, God,” answered the parson, “I have a lame foot; I cannot go out and drive him off.”
sentences.n: “wegbannen” = to banish by a spell or exorcism — the parson’s professional remedy. The verb of motion falls out after the modal again: “I cannot [go] out.”

sentences.t: Sprach der Mann „so will ich euch hockeln,“ und hockelte ihn hinaus.
sentences.l: Spoke the man “then I will carry you pick-a-back,” and carried him out on his back.
sentences.i: The man said: “Then I will carry you pick-a-back,” and carried him out on his back.
sentences.n: hockeln is a dialect verb: to carry someone on one’s back or shoulders.

sentences.t: Und als sie bei das Land kamen, machte sich das Catherlieschen auf und reckte sich in die Höhe.
sentences.l: And when they came to the land, the Catherlieschen got itself up and stretched itself up into the height.
sentences.i: And when they reached the field, Catherlieschen got up and stretched herself upright.
sentences.n: “sich aufmachen” usually means to set out; here it is literal — she gets up. bei das Land: bei with the accusative again, as the region speaks.

sentences.t: „Ach, der Teufel!“ rief der Pfarrer, und beide eilten fort, und der Pfarrer konnte vor großer Angst mit seinem lahmen Fuße gerader laufen, als der Mann, der ihn gehockt hatte, mit seinen gesunden Beinen.
sentences.l: “Ah, the devil!” called the parson, and both hurried off, and out of great fear the parson could run straighter on his lame foot than the man who had carried him could on his sound legs.
sentences.i: “Ah, the devil!” cried the parson; and both hurried away — and in his great fright the parson could run straighter on his lame foot than the man who had carried him could on two sound legs.
sentences.n: vor here = out of, from (a cause). gehockt is a clipped form of gehockelt, from the same dialect verb. The tale ends on the joke and nothing more: no reckoning, no moral, and not another word of Catherlieschen.
